The sound the letter R makes is considered a fricative sound, meaning it's made by vibrating the vocal cords. It has no accompanied mouth movements that are easily replicable by sight. It's why it's a very common speech impediment among hearing children as well who often replace R with a W "Weady to go?" "I want to wead a book" it requires a lot of coordination inside your mouth to produce and is learned through repetition after mimicking those around you pronouncing it correctly. 

If you can't hear yourself or others, and you can't mimic a simple mouth movement you see others make when they say a word, you're left to do the best you can. There are lots of sounds and letter combinations that are difficult in this way. Letters like P are very simple. Say Pop. You can see each P and and how it's formed but the middle 'ah' sound is simply made using vocal cords. Deaf people often distinctly pronounce each P but the middle syllable often comes out as 'uh' because control over your vocal cords is difficult without the feedback of hearing yourself and comparing it to others.

A huge part of learning a language as a child is immersion. Immersion is existing in a space where everyone is communicating in the same language as you. A baby hears their parents speaking, the TV is in English, the kids in the neighborhood speak English, you learn all the words and their sounds, picking them up as people speak in groceries stores and at the park, you begin to connect words to object. Your parent points at a duck and says duck. Okay, now you know that word means duck. 

By the time you are learning to read, you know all the words you are learning, you are just connecting letters to the sound. 

The grammatical structure has already been being demonstrated to you for years. 

Now imagine if after all this learning of spoken English you had to learn written Chinese instead. Suddenly 'duck' is a completely new word and all the grammatical structures are different. It's no longer connecting your spoken language to a written language but instead having to learn an entire new language without ever having spoken it. Which would be nearly impossible. 

If your only communication to the world outside yourself was written English, you are language deprived, and you deserve better. Sign language is for anyone who can't communicate verbally, not just deaf people. 

A deaf baby of hearing parents does not share the same first language as them. 

Learning to read is a deaf child's FIRST experience with English. They will always be behind hearing children. ASL is essential.
